Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of the Republic of Botswana (Botswana) who claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1 Allegations

The claimant alleges that she is lesbian by sexual orientation, which she became aware of from the age of 15. When her parents learned of her sexual orientation in XXXX 2010, they informed her of their intention to force her into marriage with a much older man. She alleges that her intended spouse raped her when she spurned his advances in XXXX 2011. She fled the family home in XXXX to move to the capital Gaborone. In XXXX 2011, she alleges that her father and hired thugs attempted to kidnap her. She escaped this attempt. She fled to Canada in December 2011, making a claim for protection upon her arrival at Pearson Airport. She alleges a well-founded fear of persecution for reason her membership in a particular social group, namely her sexual orientation and as a woman fearing forced marriage and victim of gender-related violence.

In the course of her testimony, the claimant declared that her alleged partner had forwarded to her an affidavit as well as a hospital report. She declared that this was sent by regular mail four days before the sitting on November 22, 2012. On application from counsel for the claimant, the panel agreed to wait until December 14, 2012, to receive the material, together with counsel's submissions on the merits of the claim. Although they arrived late, the documents and counsel's submissions were received and considered. 2 Issues and Determination

The panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. In reaching this decision the panel considered the Chairperson's Guidelines on women refugee claimants fearing gender related persecution.3 The determinative issue was the credibility of the claimant. The panel's reasons are as follows: Identity

The claimant's identity is disclosed by the documentation disclosed, including the certified copy of her Botswana passport, 4 for which the original is retained by the Canada Border Services Agency, as well as the claimant's birth certificate and education documents bearing her name. 5 The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's personal identity and Botswana nationality on a balance of probabilities.

It is settled law that the claimant's testimony under affirmation is presumed to be truthful, unless the panel has valid reason to doubt it.6 For the reasons that follow, the panel concludes that the claimant is neither a lesbian nor was she raped or threatened with forced marriage.

The claimant testified that her parents were horrified and appalled by alleging coming upon her and her same-sex partner engaged in sex. She says that immediately upon making this discovery her parents informed her that she would be forced into marriage. According to her testimony, however, there had been no marriage arranged when her suitor came calling 7 months later in XXXX 2011. The panel does not find it plausible that the parents would have waited 7 months to arrange a marriage when the groom was already selected in XXXX 2010.

On the question of forced marriage, a Response to Information Request(RIR) from the division declares in part: The pressures of marriage means that these children are unable to continue their education as they are being forced into adulthood and they end up being dependant on their husband for support, since they end up with no skills to earn their own income. These are some of the customs and practises that are perpetuated in spite of existing statutory laws protecting women and girls against discrimination. (ibid., 51-52)7 This does not appear to concern the claimant, who received an associate degree in Public Relations in March 2010.8 The same RIR goes on to state: In contrast, in a 2008 report on its implementation of CEDAW, Botswana authorities state that, whether under customary or common law, the choice of a spouse in "most cases" is "voluntary" (Botswana 20 Oct. 2008, para. 228). They also indicate that forced marriages take place "only in isolated instances" (ibid.). The Botswana authorities add that in those cases where marriage is forced, there has been some condemnation of the parents of involved young women, especially if they are still in school. The traditional practice of arranged marriages through betrothal (peeletso), is no longer permissible as it adversely affected women usually involved with elderly men. In such cases the girl-child has no say as the matter would have been concluded with her parents. If she is a minor, the law allows the parents to consent on her behalf.(ibid.)

However, the authorities also state that, [m]arriage officers cannot readily ascertain whether consent to marriage was given freely or not because parents are given the latitude to decide what is in the best interest of their child and if they readily consent there is no reason for the marriage officer to doubt. This practice could deny girls the right of choice and independent decision making. (ibid., para. 229)9

The United States Department of State Report declares: By law women have the same civil rights as men, but societal discrimination persisted. A number of traditional laws enforced by tribal structures and customary courts restricted women's property rights and economic opportunities, particularly in rural areas. Marriages can occur under one of three systems, each with its own implications for women's property rights. A woman married under traditional law or in "common property" is held to be a legal minor and required to have her husband's consent to buy or sell property, apply for credit, and enter into legally binding contracts. Under an intermediate system referred to as "in community of property," married women may own real estate in their own names, and the law stipulates that neither spouse can dispose of joint property without the written consent of the other. Women increasingly exercised the right to marriage "out of common property," in which they retained their full legal rights as adults.10

The claimant is university-educated and not raised in a rural environment. The only evidence disclosed from her alleged same-sex partner makes no reference to the threat of a forced marriage.11 In light of the evidence on the practise of forced marriage, and the lack of evidence to corroborate her allegation, the panel is satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not subjected to a threat of forced marriage.

The panel asked the claimant if she had reported the alleged rape to the police. She replied that she had done so but the police dismissed her complaint summarily. The documentary evidence on police response to rape, however, declares: Laws against rape were effectively enforced when victims pressed charges; however, police noted victims often declined to press charges against the perpetrators, and the extent of the problem was likely underreported. In some cases of domestic but non-spousal rape, victims were afraid of losing financial support if perpetrators were found guilty and imprisoned. The number of reported rape cases decreased during the year from 1,332 in 2010 to 1,173 in 2011 between January and September in both years. NGOs continued efforts to improve awareness of the crime. By law the minimum sentence for rape is 10 years in prison, increasing to 15 years with corporal punishment if the offender is HIV-positive, and 20 years with corporal punishment if the offender was aware of having HIV-positive status.12

The claimant alleges that she went to press charges. The documentary evidence suggests the police would have received her complaint if she had actually made it. The panel finds on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not in fact file a complaint with the police. The claimant also declared she did not seek medical attention after the alleged rape. The panel finds that implausible given the prevalence of HIV-AIDS in Botswana.

Underpinning the issues of forced marriage and the subsequent alleged rape is the question of the claimant's sexual orientation. The only evidence of the relationship is an unsigned letter from her alleged partner. She disclosed no photographs or anything else to document a relationship supposedly in existence since 2009. She testified that she hoped to sponsor her same-sex partner's immigration to Canada, and yet she has little evidence to establish the existence of this person. Post-Hearing Evidence

The claimant testified that four days before the hearing on November 22, 2012 her partner had forwarded by regular mail an affidavit and a record of hospital visit, arising from injuries sustained kidnapping in XXXX 2011. The panel notes there was no reference to the hospitalization in the Personal Information Form (PIF),13 nor was there any reference to the claimant moving house within the same district of Gaborone following the attack. She had no explanation for these omissions.

The claimant disclosed a number of documents post-hearing: a medical report dated November 19, 2012; another dated December 7, 2012, a pathology report dated March 21, 2011 and an affidavit apparently executed by XXXX XXXX on November 16 2012.14 Also disclosed was a courier envelope indicating that the parcel was accepted by the courier company on December 11, 2012, and not sent by regular mail as the claimant had testified. The panel infers that this cannot be the material the claimant alleged was in transit by regular mail on November 18, four days before the hearing on November 22, as it includes medical reports that were issued after November 18. The later medical report was issued some two weeks after the hearing was completed and after the panel confronted the claimant with the omissions in the PIF and lack of documentation. The panel gives little probative value to these documents in the circumstances. The affidavit from XXXX XXXX bore an address of XXXX, although at the time of the hearing the claimant testified that XXXX was living in XXXX. The affidavit itself adds little to a relationship which supposedly has been in existence since 2009.

Rule 715 requires the claimant to introduce documentation to establish both her identity and the other elements of her claim and to explain what steps she has taken to obtain documentation reasonably available. In the Kante decision, the Court affirmed that the claimant must come to a hearing with all of the evidence that he or she is able to offer and believes is necessary to prove the claim.16 The panel finds the claimant that she has not adequately documented a relationship allegedly subsisting since 2009. The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that she is not lesbian as alleged. She is not a Convention refugee accordingly. S. 97 - Danger of Torture

The claimant did not allege a danger of torture. The documentary evidence does not lead the panel to believe that such a danger exists.17 The panel concludes the claimant does not face a danger of torture in Botswana. S. 97 - Risk to Life, Cruel and Unusual Treatment or Punishment

In view of the panel's assessment of the credibility of the claimant, there is not sufficient objective, reliable evidence to establish a personalized risk for the claimant in Botswana. The panel is persuaded that any risk the claimant faces is one shared by other persons residing in Botswana. She is not a person in need of protection accordingly. Conclusion

The panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor is she a person in need of protection. The panel therefore rejects the present claim. (signed) "Michael S.
